issues.explanation: For stalking trauma, 'Betrayal' can be plausible if the stalker was known to the patient, but the profile provides no supporting items suggesting an interpersonal betrayal context. More importantly, 'Contamination' is typically associated with sexual assault or physical violation and is hard to reconcile clinically with stalking in the absence of any other items indicating assault, bodily intrusion, or abuse.

Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Contamination' point to different trauma meanings: interpersonal trust violation versus bodily violation. They can coexist in some cases, but with stalking alone and no corroborating memory, trigger, or threat items, this combination is clinically difficult to justify.

For stalking trauma, 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is hard to reconcile unless there was an additional sexual or physical assault element. On its face, this appraisal is clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

'Avoid Medical Care' implies avoidance centered on trauma-related examination, disclosure, or bodily injury/assault concerns, but there are no Memory, Threat, or Trigger items indicating injury, assault, or medical trauma. It is poorly matched to the rest of this stalking profile.

vignette:
Mele is a 20-year-old single woman of Oceanian background who works as a junior auditor, and when she describes the months that changed her life, she talks first about how ordinary everything had seemed at the beginning. She had been early in her job, still trying to prove herself, commuting between the office and client sites, learning to carry herself with the seriousness she thought the role required. The stalking began in the middle of that routine. At first it was only a sense that the same man was appearing too often—outside her apartment building, near the train platform she used for work, across the street when she left a café after a long day. Then the pattern became unmistakable. He was not a stranger passing by; he was watching, waiting, placing himself where she would have to notice him. For Mele, what made it terrifying was not a single dramatic confrontation but the repeated experience of realizing that someone had studied her movements closely enough to be there before she arrived. Going to work, coming home, stepping out for coffee, each ordinary act began to feel exposed.

In the weeks that followed, she came to feel that nowhere was neutral anymore. A sidewalk, a station entrance, the stretch outside her office building all seemed charged with the possibility that he would be there again. She had come to believe that the world was dangerous in a total way, not just that one person was dangerous. Being outside no longer felt like moving through normal life; it felt like entering a place where she had to scan constantly. She noticed faces, footsteps, parked cars, reflections in windows. If someone slowed near her, if she caught a glimpse of a man standing too still, her whole attention narrowed around it. She was certain she had to stay on guard all the time. Even when nothing happened, she did not relax. The absence of immediate threat never meant safety to her; it only meant she had not yet spotted where danger was.

Mele’s work as an auditor kept placing her in exactly the kinds of settings she now dreaded. She still had to enter unfamiliar office buildings, leave after dusk during busy periods, and cross parking lots or walk from transit stops to client sites. Colleagues might chat casually on the way out, but Mele’s attention was usually elsewhere, checking who was behind her, who had come through the lobby, whether anyone was lingering outside. Over time she began avoiding going out whenever she could. Outside of what she viewed as absolutely necessary work obligations, she stayed in. She turned down invitations, skipped errands until she could not put them off any longer, and structured her days around minimizing time beyond her door. Her world grew smaller and more controlled, which to her felt like the only sensible response.

The change was visible to people around her even when she said little. Friends stopped asking as often when she repeatedly declined plans. At work, she remained conscientious, but the effort of getting herself to each site had become enormous, and she no longer moved through the job with the optimism she once had. Situations that might have made her feel happy or hopeful began to feel almost intolerable. If someone suggested dinner after work, a weekend outing, or anything that carried the possibility of lightness, she pulled back from it. Part of her felt she should not have those moments. She told herself she deserved to suffer because of what had happened. She did not frame this as self-pity; it was harsher than that, more like a private verdict. Pleasure felt wrong, as if letting herself enjoy anything would mean forgetting what had been done to her or admitting she had not been ruined by it.

By the time she sought help, Mele spoke about the stalking as something that had destroyed her life. She did not mean only that she had been frightened. She meant that the person she had been before—young, ambitious, willing to go where work took her, open to simple plans—felt unreachable now. Her days were organized around vigilance and restriction, and she viewed that as realism rather than overreaction. What finally brought her in was the recognition that she could no longer imagine living this way indefinitely. She was exhausted by being on guard and hemmed in by how little of life she allowed herself, yet she was also frightened of what it would mean to loosen any of it. What she fears most is that the danger she senses is still everywhere and that she will be caught off guard if she lets herself live normally again. What she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is to get through a workday, step outside, and not feel as if the whole world is waiting to harm her.
